questions.q: What does the DATE type store?
options: Time of day only, no date
A calendar date only — year, month, day, with no time component
Only the year
Both date and time together
questions.explain: DATE is appropriate for values like a birth date, where a time-of-day would be meaningless.

questions.q: What is DATETIME's valid date range limitation?
options: It cannot store dates before January 1, 1753
It can only store dates in the current year
It cannot store any date after the year 2000
DATETIME has no range limitation at all
questions.explain: This is one of DATETIME's well-known legacy quirks.

questions.q: What precision issue does DATETIME have?
options: It only stores whole minutes
It has no precision issues compared to DATETIME2
It rounds to increments of about 3.33 milliseconds, not a clean fraction of a second
It cannot store fractional seconds at all
questions.explain: DATETIME2 fixes this with genuinely precise fractional seconds.

questions.q: Why is DATETIME2 recommended over DATETIME for new development?
options: DATETIME2 uses less storage in every case
DATETIME is no longer supported at all in SQL Server
DATETIME2 is required for use with WHERE clauses
DATETIME2 has a much wider valid date range and true fractional-second precision
questions.explain: DATETIME2 fixes both of DATETIME's legacy limitations, though DATETIME still appears constantly in existing databases like AdventureWorks2012.

questions.q: Why does storing a birth date as DATETIME (instead of DATE) invite confusion?
options: DATETIME cannot store dates before 1900
There is no meaningful difference — this is purely a style preference
It implies a time-of-day that doesn't actually exist or mean anything for a birth date
DATETIME requires a separate TIME column to work correctly
questions.explain: This mirrors the CHAR/VARCHAR lesson — picking the narrowest appropriate type communicates intent and avoids ambiguity later.
